system-calls.name: System Calls — How Programs Talk to the OS
system-calls.desc: A system call is how a user program requests a service from the kernel. Examples: open() (open a file), read() (read data), write() (write data), fork() (create a process), exit() (terminate). Every file operation, network call, or memory allocation goes through a syscall.
system-calls.qsub: What is the cost of a system call? What happens at the CPU level when a syscall is made (trap/interrupt mechanism)?
system-calls.what:
When an app needs to perform an OS task — open a file, read data, create a new process, get the time — it cannot do it directly (low privilege). It makes a system call.

Think of read() as: the app asks the kernel "give me data from this file". The kernel reads it and returns the result to the app.
system-calls.analogy: In school, a peon pass: the child (app) wants to go to the library but cannot go on its own. It gets a teacher (kernel) pass — the teacher checks if it is allowed, then the child goes. Every major task requires the teacher's permission.
system-calls.why: If every app had full control over files/disks/network on its own, it could steal other users' data or damage hardware. The system call is a barrier — the kernel checks each request before granting it (allowed? safe?). This provides both security and safety.
pros: Hardware usage is controlled and safe.
The app doesn't need to manage hardware details.
The kernel checks every request (permission).
cons: Each syscall adds overhead — context switch + boundary.
Many syscalls can slow the program down (batching).
The complexity of understanding syscalls (privacy, data copy).
gotchas: Just remember: system call = app asking the kernel "do this for me" — cannot access hardware directly.
"Why is a syscall costly?" = Ring 3→Ring 0 switch + data copy + return.
Interview: "how to read a file?" = read() syscall → kernel → disk → back.
terms: App's request to the kernel — "perform this hardware operation for me".
The hardware door through which the app reaches the kernel (Ring 3 to Ring 0).
Save the app's state, load the kernel, then return.
where: "How does a program talk to hardware?" — answer: system call.

types-of-os.q: What are the different types of operating systems? Give a real-world example of each.
types-of-os.qsub: What is the difference between a general-purpose OS and a real-time OS? Why can you not use Linux to control a pacemaker?
types-of-os.what:
Operating systems are built for different tasks. The type is determined by — which aspect is most important.

Batch — submit work first, the machine processes everything together, then gives the result. (Old card-punch era.)

Time-sharing — the OS on your desktop PC. Multiple users/programs, each gets a slice of time, everyone feels like they are the main one.

Real-time — strict deadline. A monitor needs an answer within 2 ms, otherwise the patient is at risk.

Other categories: Mobile (power-saving, touch) and Distributed (many machines working together).
types-of-os.analogy:
Two restaurant modes:
• Batch — you write down the order and give it, the kitchen collects all orders and prepares them together, and only then you get the plate.
• Time-sharing — a single chef prepares each table’s order a little at a time, making everyone feel their dish is being prepared.
• Real-time — in an ICU, when the monitor beeps, the nurse must arrive immediately — no room for delay.
types-of-os.why: One OS does not fit everyone. Bank servers need high throughput. ICUs / flights need precise timing. Hence different OSes — each task has its primary requirement.
pros: Everyone gets a time slice (time-sharing, fair).
Real-time safety — immediate response in emergencies.
Distributed = as powerful as a large computer.
cons: Batch is slow, no interaction/back-and-forth.
In real-time both hardware and software are expensive (must be reliable).
Distributed systems have challenges: synchronization, network failures.
gotchas: Just remember: Time-sharing = small time slices for everyone, Real-time = a fixed deadline.
"You cannot run a heart pacemaker using Linux" — because a general OS may miss deadlines.
Interview: "difference between general and RTOS?" = the deadline is the real answer.
terms: Submit work first, then process it all together — no interaction.
Give a single CPU small time slices to many users so everyone feels it’s theirs.
Multiple computers work together as one, appearing as a single system to the user.
OS designed for small devices (phone/tablet) — Android, iOS.
where: iOS/Android = mobile OS (built on the Linux kernel).

what-is-os.qsub: What would happen if there was no OS and two programs both tried to write to the disk at the same time?
what-is-os.what:
The computer's real body (hardware) is — CPU, RAM, disk. But when you open something like chrome, it cannot talk directly to the CPU/disk.

In between, the OS stands. Its job: to allocate the hardware's time/resources to all programs, so each program feels like it is alone. In short: OS = hardware's manager and programs' friend.
what-is-os.analogy: Hotel manager. All staff (programs) want to cook, but there is only one kitchen (hardware). The manager decides who, when, how much gas, how much time to use. Without a manager, everyone would say "me first!" and the kitchen would break.
what-is-os.why: If there is no OS, two programs could write to the disk at the same time — erasing each other's data. Or they could both grab the CPU. The OS exists so that all programs get safe and equal time, and no one tampers with another's data.
pros: Programs don't interact directly with the hardware.
Each program feels like it is running alone.
If one program misbehaves, it doesn't crash the whole computer (safety).
cons: The OS is also software — new version upgrades are expensive.
Requesting the OS for every operation (syscall) takes a little time.
Bugs in the OS affect the entire system.
gotchas: Just remember: The OS doesn't cook biryani itself; it is the chef that takes raw ingredients (CPU, RAM) and serves them.

kernel.name: Kernel — The Core of the OS
kernel.desc: The kernel is the core program that runs at all times. It manages CPU, memory, devices, and files. User space = where your apps run. Kernel space = where the OS runs. Apps cannot touch hardware directly — they ask the kernel.
kernel.q: What is the kernel? What is the difference between user space and kernel space?
kernel.qsub: What are CPU privilege levels (Ring 0 vs Ring 3)? Why does the hardware enforce this separation?
kernel.what:
The OS is not a single thing — its core is the kernel. Like the head chef in a restaurant staff.

Inside the CPU there is a rule: your normal program (app) gets low privilege — it cannot touch hardware directly. Only the kernel, which runs with high privilege, uses the hardware directly.

When an app needs hardware (e.g., write to disk), it makes a request to the kernel. This is called a system call.
kernel.analogy: At a railway station, the big officer is the TCO (Train Control). The driver (app) cannot change signals directly. It tells the TCO, "I need to go to the platform," as a request — the TCO (kernel) changes the track. That’s why two drivers don’t end up on the same track.
kernel.why: For safety. If every app could touch hardware directly — a single app could accidentally erase all the computer’s data. The kernel exists to check and decide — "whether you are allowed to access this file or not."
pros: Direct control over hardware — fast and powerful.
Protects apps from hardware complexity (safe).
Multiple apps can share the same hardware.
cons: A kernel bug = whole system crash.
System call overhead (time for each request).
The kernel itself is complex and heavy.
gotchas: Just remember: Kernel = OS core, high privilege, hardware in its hands. App = low privilege, makes requests.
"Now it’s kernel space vs user space" — saying Ring 0 vs Ring 3 feels right.
Running your own code on the kernel (module) = risk to the whole system.
terms: OS core — talks directly to hardware, resides in memory at all times.
Where your apps run (web browsers, games).
Where the OS runs — full control over hardware.
CPU’s division of power — who can use how much authority (Ring 0 = OS, Ring 3 = app).
where: Like the Linux kernel, Windows NT kernel — the core of every OS.
Ring 0 vs Ring 3 — this is how apps are restricted from the internet.
"user space vs kernel space?" — answer the direct difference.
kernel.visualCap: App runs with low privilege — cannot access hardware directly. Kernel runs with high privilege — can do everything.

boot-process.desc: Power on → BIOS/UEFI (hardware check, find boot device) → Bootloader (GRUB loads kernel) → Kernel (initializes drivers, mounts filesystem) → Init/systemd (starts system services) → Login shell / Desktop. This is what happens before you see the login screen.
boot-process.q: Explain what happens from the moment you press the power button to when the OS is ready.
boot-process.what:
Press power → from start to OS ready is a single line:

1. Power on → BIOS/UEFI performs hardware check (RAM/disk on), finds the boot device.

2. Bootloader (GRUB) — extracts the kernel from disk into memory, then runs it.

3. Kernel — starts itself: loads drivers (keyboard, disk), mounts filesystem (prepares disk), sets up memory.

4. init/systemd — first user-space process; the rest of the services (wifi, sound) are its children.

5. Login screen — now you can log in.
boot-process.analogy:
Morning waking sequence:
1. As soon as you wake, check — water, electricity (BIOS).
2. Take out the school bag — the books you need (bootloader pulls the kernel).
3. Teacher arrives to manage the class (kernel init).
4. Monitor/children register (systemd) and other services start.
5. Bell — you start work (login).
boot-process.why: Because a computer cannot jump straight to the OS — the hardware does not automatically invoke the OS. The CPU must first decide: what to do, where to find the kernel on the disk, how to set up memory. This sequence ensures that everything happens in the correct order — otherwise the computer would fail.
pros: Order guaranteed — everything knows what runs first.
Hardware checked first (hot boot = immediate failure).
systemd = a parent that manages all services.
cons: Many steps — if one fails, boot breaks.
BIOS/UEFI themselves have complex setup.
In dual-boot, the bootloader update must be done correctly.
gotchas: Just remember: Power → BIOS → Bootloader → Kernel → init → Login.
UEFI is new & secure, BIOS is old — mention the difference in interviews.
Running update-grub makes GRUB show the new OS.
terms: Computer's first software that "wakes up" the machine — OS is not running yet.
Small program that loads the kernel into memory and runs it (GRUB).
When the kernel starts — it sets up drivers, filesystem, memory.
First OS service — all other background processes are its children.
New BIOS — fast, safer (secure boot). The old BIOS.
where: GRUB — asks the user which OS to boot.
If the boot fails (black screen), you need to repair the GRUB bootloader.
"From power to login?" — answer using this 5-step sequence.

process-vs-thread.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread? What resources does each own?
process-vs-thread.qsub: Why is creating a thread much cheaper than creating a process? What does fork() do under the hood?
process-vs-thread.what:
Process = a small "house" where a program lives. If you run two programs, you get two separate houses — one has no idea what’s inside the other’s house.

Thread = a worker inside the same house. Many people (threads) can live in one house, all sharing the same kitchen (memory).

The only difference: a process does not share the house, a thread shares the house.
process-vs-thread.analogy: Rainy day — a house with 3 brothers (threads). All share the same kitchen, so if one makes tea, all three will drink it. The neighbor next door (another process) has a separate kitchen; we cannot touch it.
process-vs-thread.why: A web page is a process. If a single person handled the entire page, a heavy task would freeze the page. Therefore the browser keeps multiple threads — one thread handles the UI, another handles the network.
pros: Processes are separate — if one crashes, the other stays safe.
Threads are cheap — no need to build a new house, just share the kitchen.
Process = safety, Thread = speed.
cons: Two processes cannot signal each other directly (need IPC).
If a thread makes a mistake, the whole process can crash.
Coordinating threads (synchronization) is difficult.
gotchas: Just remember: process = separate house, thread = same house. Everything else follows from that.
"Is a Web Worker a virtual thread?" — No, they are real OS threads, just created through the browser.
In an interview say: a process has its own memory, a thread shares memory — that’s the direct answer.
terms: A program that is running in memory. It has its own house (memory), its own papers (files), everything of its own.
A worker inside a process. A process can have many threads, all living in the same house.
When multiple threads access the same thing, everything still works correctly.
where: Heavy computation worker thread to keep the UI from freezing.
Background thread of the browser — notifications, caching.
"On a page with two heavy tasks — why does the main thread freeze?" — answer: both run on the same thread.

pcb.desc: Data structure the OS maintains for each process — PID, state, CPU registers, memory maps, open files.
pcb.q: What information is stored in a Process Control Block? Why does the OS need it?
pcb.what:
OS has to keep complete information about each process — not just the name, everything. This information resides in a packed file, which is called a PCB.

When a process is created (an app opens), the OS gives it a PCB — like a file created at school admission.
pcb.analogy: The school office keeps a file for each student — name, roll number, marks, what mischief they did. When the student (process) is working, the entire file is with the office (OS).
pcb.why: The CPU leaves one process for another (context switch). When it returns, it needs to know where it left off. The PCB is that note — "left here, resume here."
pros: All information about a process is in one place — the OS doesn't have to search.
The CPU knows where to resume.
Debugging/management is easy.
cons: PCBs consume memory (a little for each process).
Managing the PCB list itself is a task.
The full structure of all information must be remembered.
gotchas: Just remember: PCB = a file for a process that contains its entire state (where it is, where it left off).
Context switch = loading/unloading CPU registers to/from the PCB.
In an interview, don't list every field — say: identity + state + registers + files + memory.

context-switching.desc: The OS saves the current process state and loads another process state — enables multitasking but has overhead.
context-switching.what:
The CPU does only one task at a time, but we need to show that the computer runs everything simultaneously.

The trick is: the CPU very quickly drops one process, grabs another, then grabs the first again. Every time it "drops" it writes a note — I was here up to this point. Writing that note and reading the other note is what a context switch is.
context-switching.analogy: Several people are reading books together, but there is only one chair. Whenever someone leaves the chair, they place a bookmark on the page of their book. Switching seats takes about 2 seconds (overhead), but everyone feels like they are all reading.
context-switching.why: Without it, if you run one app, everything else will freeze (stop). Context switching is the magic of multitasking — the switch happens so fast that you don’t notice it.
pros: Multiple apps can run on a single CPU.
Each process gets a little bit of time.
The user perceives everything as responsive.
cons: Each switch incurs overhead (time waste).
More switches = more waste — "context switch thrash".
Thread switches are cheap, process switches are expensive (memory also has to be changed).
gotchas: Just remember: context switch = leaving a bookmark, picking up another's book.
Process switch > thread switch overhead — because the entire memory map of the process must be changed.

process-states.q: Describe the lifecycle of a process. Draw the state diagram and explain each transition.
process-states.what:
Every process has a small "life" — several phases that occur one after another:

New (created) → Ready (ready, but waiting) → Running (CPU assigned) → Waiting (waiting for something) → Running back → Terminated (finished).

The most important transition: Running ⇄ Waiting. When a process waits for I/O (for example reading a file), the CPU releases it and gives the CPU to another process.
process-states.analogy: In a bank there is one counter, many customers. Every customer is in Waiting (queue). When the counter is free, one becomes Running. If that customer needs a passport copy (I/O) that will arrive in 2 minutes — they move to Waiting, and the counter is given to another. When the copy arrives, they go back to the queue.
process-states.why: The CPU should not sit idle. When a process pareshan (I/O wait), release it and give the CPU to another process. This keeps the CPU at "100% work", no one stays idle.
pros: The state tells you what the process is currently doing.
CPU does not stay idle — give it to another process during I/O wait.
The diagram is easy to remember — just 4-5 boxes.
cons: The state can change in real hardware at any moment (race conditions).
Remembering many states and transitions is difficult.
Real OSes have many sub-states and queues.
gotchas: Just remember: Running ⇄ Waiting is the gate where I/O occurs.
Waiting means separated from the processor. It is also called "blocked".
Interview: "How many times does a process go from Running to Waiting?" — on every I/O/sleep.

user-vs-kernel-threads.q: What is the difference between user-level and kernel-level threads? What are green threads?
user-vs-kernel-threads.qsub: Node.js uses a single kernel thread but handles concurrency. How? How does the thread pool in libuv help?
user-vs-kernel-threads.what:
There are two types of threads:

Kernel thread — created by the OS. It gets a real CPU core and can run on multiple cores simultaneously. Creation (syscall) takes a little time.

User thread — managed inside the program by the runtime. Creation is cheap, execution is fast — but if a task blocks (I/O), the risk is that the entire program can stop (if one thread blocks, all block).
user-vs-kernel-threads.analogy: Kernel thread = your own worker that talks directly to the OS and can dispatch many tasks to separate cores. User thread = household members who divide work themselves — fast, but if one person gets stuck (I/O) the whole house can stop.
user-vs-kernel-threads.why: User threads are fast because they don’t need to ask the OS each time. Kernel threads are necessary because they get real CPU cores. A balance of both is needed.
pros: User thread cheap & fast — no syscall.
User thread can handle hundreds of thousands of tasks on a single thread.
Kernel thread utilizes real multicore.
cons: User thread: if one blocks, all block (blocking I/O).
The OS doesn’t recognize green threads — no scheduler.
Kernel thread creation is expensive (syscall).
gotchas: Just remember: user thread = runtime’s toy (fast, single place); kernel thread = OS’s worker (slower, gets cores).
JS is single-threaded — but async I/O and networking work well because they follow a "user thread" model.
Interview: "Why is Node fast? concurrency is all non-blocking." — that’s the green thread model.
terms: Created by the OS — can use CPU cores. Heavy, but important.
Thread inside the program — depends on the OS (diesel).
User thread that the runtime manages itself (as in JS/Python).
where: The main thread is a user thread; libuv’s thread pool uses kernel threads.
"Why isn’t JS thread-safe?" — single user thread, so races don’t occur.

fork-exec.what:
The process needs to do a new task (like running a good program).

Two steps are required:

1. fork() — create a "copy of the game" (a new process). Now there are two identical programs — parent and child.

2. exec() — replace the old code inside that new copy with a new program. The child's job becomes different.

In short: to start a new thing, fork and then exec.
fork-exec.analogy: Make a photocopy of a book (fork) — now there are two pages with the same content. Then tear one page and WRITE the new book's content on it (exec). The photocopy is cheap because the actual copying happens only when something changes (copy-on-write).
fork-exec.why: The OS wants a "cheap copy" for the new program rather than creating a "brand-new empty world" — building an empty world is expensive. So it first makes a copy (fork, cheap), then swaps in a part (exec). That's it.

stack-vs-heap.what:
When a program runs, it gets memory in two parts:

Stack — the fastest. On every function call a "frame" is placed on top, and removed as soon as it returns. LIFO (last in, first out) — one on top of another. Automatic, no one deletes it manually.

Heap — the largest. Here you request memory yourself (object, array) in any order. Slow, and you have to free it yourself (GC or manually).
stack-vs-heap.analogy:
Plate stack (stack) — always keep on top, remove from the top. Fast and fixed.
Store-room (heap) — place any item in any corner, take it when needed. Large space, but no ordering rule — many empty spots scattered.
stack-vs-heap.why: The stack is fast because it is simply that way — just push/pop, no bookkeeping. The heap exists so that large & dynamic data (whose size isn’t known beforehand) can reside there. Each has its own purpose — so they are separate.

virtual-memory.what:
Every program thinks that its entire RAM belongs only to it — for example from 0 to 4GB, all of it is theirs.

But this is false. The OS creates a virtual address space — a fake, safe, larger space where the program runs. The real RAM is elsewhere.

Page table is the translator that tells: "your data at 0x4000 is actually in RAM at 0x9000." The program does not care about the real world. This provides isolation — one program cannot see another program's memory.
virtual-memory.analogy: In a large warehouse (RAM), many people work on separate shelves. Everyone is given a map (page table) that shows where their item is. No one can look at another's shelf (isolation), and no one worries about the real layout. If an item is outside the warehouse (disk), the map later reports "now found" (page fault).
virtual-memory.why: Two major benefits: (1) Isolation — a program's mistake does not corrupt another program's data. (2) Larger programs — programs can appear larger than physical memory because the unused portion can reside on disk (if more than RAM is needed).

paging.qsub: What is the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)? Why is it critical for performance?
paging.what:
Divide memory into small same-size blocks (like pages of a book). The block on the virtual side is called a page, and the block on the physical (RAM) side is called a frame.

Page table tells which page resides in which frame. When a program accesses a page that is not in RAM (it is on disk), a page fault occurs — the OS fetches it from disk into RAM, then the program continues.

paging.why: Paging provides isolation and flexibility. Not all pages of a program need to be in RAM — only the needed ones are loaded. This allows large programs to run on small RAM. And fixed-size blocks eliminate external fragmentation (no need to search for a large free region).

segmentation.what:
Paging divides memory into fixed blocks, but segmentation divides it into logical parts — code, data, stack as separate segments.

Each segment has its own base (where it starts) and limit (how long it is). The program address is written as: (segmentNo, offset). The hardware checks — if offset < limit is not true, a segfault occurs!

Unlike paging where blocks are fixed, segments can be small or large — therefore external fragmentation occurs (scattered free space).
segmentation.analogy: Paging = all drawers are the same size. Segmentation = each item has its own separate container — a box for the recipe, a box for spices, a box for vegetables. Each box has its own size and label (base+limit). If you need to place a new large box and there is no contiguous free space, you get a problem (fragmentation).
segmentation.why: Logical grouping: the program knows that code, data, and stack are separate — segmentation provides that structure in memory as well. Each segment also has its own limit, so if the program accesses an incorrect offset, a immediate error (segfault) occurs — preventing data corruption. However, drawback: sizes differ, leading to scattered free space.

page-replacement.desc: When RAM is full and a new page is needed, the OS must evict one. FIFO, LRU, LFU, Clock algorithm.
page-replacement.qsub: Why is LRU difficult to implement in hardware? What is the Clock algorithm and why is it a practical approximation?
page-replacement.what:
When RAM becomes full and a new page is needed, the OS must evict an old page. Which one should it evict? That is the page replacement strategy.

FIFO — remove the one that arrived first. Simple but not optimal.

LRU — remove the least recently used. Best, because the one that won’t be needed soon is removed. However, tracking time in actual hardware is expensive.

Clock — a practical version of LRU: each page has a "use bit". All pages are arranged in a circle; when a page's bit is 0, evict it, otherwise clear the bit and continue.
page-replacement.analogy:
Office paper tray is full; to add a new sheet, which one should be removed?
• FIFO: remove the one that was placed first (even if it is currently in use).
• LRU: remove the one that was used least recently (and is not needed now) — more intelligent.
page-replacement.why: If the wrong page is evicted (the one that will be needed soon), it will immediately fault again — causing the system to experience repeated page faults: thrashing. Therefore selecting the correct page to evict is essential — evict the page that "is not needed now" in LRU style.

FIFO is simple, easy to implement.

memory-leaks.qsub: Explain the mark-and-sweep algorithm. What is a stop-the-world pause and why is it a problem for latency?
memory-leaks.what:
Leak = memory you allocated, but never returned when it is no longer used. The program keeps running while holding onto those objects.

In GC-enabled languages (JS, Java, Go) the GC automatically finds what is no longer used (unreachable) and frees it. Mark & sweep: start from the root (global) and mark everything reachable; anything not marked is freed.

However, the GC cannot prevent a leak if an object is still reachable (e.g., data stored in a global array).
memory-leaks.analogy: In a store-room, someone keeps bringing new items but never puts the old ones in the waste bin. Items (memory) fill every house. The GC is like a cleaner that looks for "things that are no longer useful (no one points to them)" and discards them. But if an item is still linked to something, the cleaner won’t discard it — and that is the real leak.
memory-leaks.why: A leak gradually fills the program’s memory → degradation, crash, or the OS kills it (OOM). Therefore you should understand: in manual languages (C) you must free yourself, while GC relies on reachability. Also watch out for closures and global hooks.

scheduling-goals.q: What are the goals of CPU scheduling? What trade-offs exist between throughput and latency?
scheduling-goals.qsub: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
scheduling-goals.what:
The scheduler's job: which process runs on the CPU and when. But "best" depends on the situation — therefore we define goals.

System goals: keep the CPU busy (utilization), do more work (throughput). User goals: finish work quickly (turnaround), get the first answer immediately (response). All of these involve a trade-off — improving one goal can degrade another.
scheduling-goals.analogy: Imagine a chef (CPU) with a kitchen that gets many orders (processes). Goals: the kitchen should never be empty (utilization), serve as many orders as possible (throughput), have each order ready quickly (turnaround), and give the customer the first bite promptly (response). All cannot happen simultaneously — so the chef decides what is most important at any moment.
scheduling-goals.why: Without goals, the scheduler runs processes arbitrarily — some processes may starve, and the CPU may sit idle. Goals let the designer decide which strategy to use — background batch, interactive desktop, or real-time, each with different goals.

Understanding the trade-off lets you balance delay and throughput.
The distinction between system and user goals shows what kind of system it is.
cons: Optimizing one goal can harm another.
Real workloads are mixed — a single policy does not fit all.
Balancing response and throughput is tricky.

fcfs-sjf.q: Compare FCFS and SJF. What is the convoy effect? Why is SJF optimal but impractical?
fcfs-sjf.what:
FCFS — the simplest. Whichever process arrived first at the market gets the CPU. Order = arrival order. The problem: if one long process comes, everyone behind it waits — the convoy effect (a traffic jam).

SJF — shortest job first. This makes the average wait time optimal. But the problem: you don't know the future (which one will be how long), and if short ones keep arriving, the big one starves to death.

SRTF — the preemptive version of SJF: whenever a new shorter one arrives, stop the running process and give it the CPU.
fcfs-sjf.analogy:
Billing/ATM line:
• FCFS — first in line, first served. If the person ahead has a 10-minute task and everyone behind has 1-minute tasks, you will wait 10 minutes (convoy).
• SJF — serve the smallest task first. The line clears quickly (optimal), but if short tasks keep arriving, the long one may never get a turn (starvation).
fcfs-sjf.why: FCFS is realistic but wasteful (convoy). SJF is best for average waiting time but has the problem of future prediction and starvation. Both clarify concepts — preemption, optimality, starvation, aging — which are also used in other algorithms.

round-robin.what:
Round Robin — each process is given a fixed time quantum, then the next one. The order is circular — after the last it returns to the first.

Each process gets equal time — no one is left starving. Therefore it is best for interactive/time-sharing. But choose the quantum wisely: too small → many context switches (overhead), too large → becomes FCFS.

round-robin.why: When response time needs to be fair and predictable, Round Robin is best — no process holds the CPU for many seconds. This is what desktops/UI need: each app gets a little bit of CPU all the time. Time-sharing systems run on this principle.

priority-scheduling.qsub: How does Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) work? What is the nice value?
priority-scheduling.what:
Priority scheduling — each process has a priority; the highest-priority one runs first. But the risk: a low-priority process may never get CPU → starvation. The remedy is aging — increase priority the longer it waits, so it eventually gets CPU.

In real systems there are multilevel queues — multiple queues with different priorities, each queue having its own policy (RR at the front, FCFS at the back). And feedback — if a process uses a lot of CPU (CPU-bound) lower its priority so that interactive processes get a chance.
priority-scheduling.analogy: Hospital emergency triage — the critical (higher priority) cases are handled first. But if only high-priority patients keep arriving, a low-priority patient may never see a doctor (starvation). Aging = “you have waited long enough, now raise your priority.” Feedback = a patient who stays in ICU for a long time (CPU-bound) is moved to a general ward (lower priority) to make room for urgent cases.
priority-scheduling.why: Real systems run different types of processes — interactive (UI, typing), batch (rendering, compilation), background (downloads). Applying the same policy to all is wrong. real-time-scheduling.q: What is the difference between hard and soft real-time systems? What is Earliest Deadline First?
real-time-scheduling.what:
Real-time = every task has a deadline. Hard: if the deadline is missed the system fails (brake system, pacemaker). Soft: if missed the quality degrades (video call, game) — but the system keeps running.

Algorithms: RMS — the one that repeats quickly (short period) gets high priority. EDF — the task with the earliest deadline always runs first; it is optimal (if any schedule is possible EDF will find it). However EDF must track deadlines continuously.
real-time-scheduling.analogy:
Delivery company's scheduler:
• Hard deadline: an oxygen cylinder must be delivered within 2 hours — missing it endangers the patient. This requires earliest-deadline scheduling (EDF).
• Soft deadline: pizza in 30 min on a best-effort basis — the customer is still happy at 35 min (a bit late). RMS = the slot that repeats most frequently gets higher priority (like a daily delivery route).
real-time-scheduling.why: Normal scheduling (fair share) does not consider deadlines — therefore real-time systems need their own scheduler that provides deadline guarantees. In hard systems the guarantee is essential. The proof that EDF is optimal is important because it underpins scheduler design.

file-system-basics.what:
Data on a disk is stored as raw bytes. The file system organizes it — files (named byte sequences) and directories (which link files/dirs to a parent).

journaling.qsub: What is the difference between data journaling and metadata-only journaling?
journaling.what:
On a file system, multiple writes need to happen together (inode + data block + directory). If power is lost in the middle, some parts are written and some are not → corruption.

Journaling: write the changes first to a log (journal), then to the actual location. When a crash occurs, the OS looks at the journal and either completes it or rolls it back — consistent state.

journaling.analogy: During a Formula 1 race, every action is first "right to repair/review" — write in the HEADER what is being changed. Crash = engine stops. By looking at the journal you know what was incomplete — you can complete or undo it. Without a journal, an incomplete operation leads to record corruption. Like a to-do list: write the list first, then do the work; if you stop midway, the list shows what happened.
journaling.why: Data is important to you. Crashes / power cuts are common. Without journaling, file system checks (fsck) took hours and data could be lost. Journal = speed vs safety: log first, then apply — a bit slower, but crash-safe. That’s why modern file systems (ext4, NTFS) all use journaling.

disk-scheduling.what:
HDD has a read/write head that must move from one track to another — this movement is called a seek and it is the slowest operation. A disk scheduler orders requests so that the head moves as little as possible.

FCFS — serve as soon as it arrives (simple, but the head moves a lot). SSTF — serve the closest request first (fast, but not completely optimal). SSTF = serves the nearest floor first — very fast, but distant floors wait (starvation possible).
disk-scheduling.why: Because HDDs are slow, reducing seek makes I/O faster. The scheduling order only optimizes seek time. However, fairness is also needed (no starvation) — therefore SCAN/C-SCAN use an elevator style: both speed and fairness. In SSDs the seek time is zero (no head), so scheduling has little impact.

pipes.why: Processes have separate memory — direct sharing is not possible. A pipe is a simple, safe way: data is sent through the kernel, no race conditions. It is the backbone of shell scripting — feeding one command’s output into another.

blocking-nonblocking-io.qsub: What is the difference between non-blocking I/O, async I/O (AIO), and I/O multiplexing (select/poll/epoll)?
blocking-nonblocking-io.what:
Blocking I/O: when you call read() the thread stops until data arrives — simple, but one thread per request (expensive).

Non-blocking I/O: read() returns immediately — if data is ready it returns it, otherwise it says "would block". The thread is not busy.

I/O multiplexing: a single thread monitors multiple fds with select/epoll — "which are ready?" — and reads only the ready ones. This is the basis of high-concurrency engines (Node, Nginx) — one thread handling thousands of connections.
blocking-nonblocking-io.analogy:
Restaurant server (thread):
• Blocking: server stands in front of each table until the order is ready — one table at a time (slow, many servers).
• Non-blocking + multiplexing: a server gives an order, moves to the next table immediately; whenever the kitchen signals "table 5 ready" (event) — it serves that table. One server, many tables. This is the Node/Nginx model.
blocking-nonblocking-io.why: All of them involve I/O wait — network, disk. If a thread stops on wait, then 10k connections = 10k threads = memory explosion. Therefore non-blocking + multiplexing lets the wait float on a single thread — high concurrency, fewer resources. Backpressure: when the sink is slow the source pauses — prevents buffer overflow.

Non-blocking code is complex (callbacks/async).

epoll.desc: Monitor many file descriptors simultaneously without polling. The basis of Node.js, Nginx, Redis event loops.
epoll.qsub: How does Node.js's libuv use epoll under the hood? Why can Node.js handle 10k concurrent connections on one thread?
epoll.what:
epoll is Linux's way to monitor many file descriptors simultaneously — "which one is ready?" The kernel knows which fds are ready, and gives you only the ready ones. Better than select/poll: they scan the entire list each time (O(n)); epoll is O(1) — it finds events on the kernel interest list.

Level-triggered — notifies as long as data is ready, on every epoll_wait. Edge-triggered — only on state change; you must read all the data (otherwise you miss it).

This is the foundation of libuv (Node) and Nginx — a single event loop handling 10k+ connections.
epoll.analogy: Gym's counter / bell system: select/poll = you check every locker each minute (O(n), inefficient). epoll = you register which lockers are of interest; when one becomes ready, the OS rings — "locker 5 ready!" (O(1), event). Level = the sound continues as long as items are inside; Edge = the sound occurs only once when opened — then you must retrieve the items yourself.
epoll.why: With select/poll, 10k connections mean scanning a list of 10k fds on every event — slow. epoll keeps a kernel-side interest list and returns only ready fds — better responsiveness and scalability. Node, Nginx, and Redis run on this. In an interview, epoll is the answer to "how Node handles 10k connections".
gotchas: Just remember: epoll = kernel-side interest list, ready events O(1). select/poll = scans every time O(n).
Level vs edge: level notifies as long as data is present; edge notifies only once (read everything).
Interview: "why can Node handle 10k?" — non-blocking + epoll event loop.

os-design-web-server.what:
High-concurrency web server design = OS primitives choose. Three models:

1. Multi-process (Apache prefork) — Each request is a process (fork). Isolation is best but heavy — 10k conns = 10k processes (memory blast).

2. Multi-thread (Apache worker) — Each request is a thread. Lighter (shared memory) but concurrency bugs risk. 10k threads are also memory-heavy.

3. Event-driven (Nginx/Io node) — Few threads + non-blocking I/O + epoll. A single event loop handles thousands of connections with a "ready-event". 10k+ connections, low memory. This is the modern answer.
os-design-web-server.analogy: Restaurant: process model = each table has a full kitchen (isolated but heavy, 100 tables = 100 kitchens). thread = each table has a cook who uses a shared pantry (lighter, but chaotic race). event-driven = 1–2 chefs, order note, "ready" bell (event) to serve — even if there are 1,000 tables, the chef doesn’t stop, just recognizes ready orders and serves repeatedly (epoll).
os-design-web-server.why: In a system-design interview, you need to choose this: "100k concurrent connections". Process/thread per request does not scale (memory). Event-driven + epoll is the realistic solution. These concepts (fork, thread, epoll, non-blocking) connect OS knowledge to design — the real "how would you build X" answer.
gotchas: Just remember: process per request = heavy isolated; thread = lighter shared; event+epoll = 1 loop, 10k connections.
Typical mix: few workers + event loop (Nginx) = balance.
Interview: "why not thread per req at 100k" — memory & race.
terms: A new process (fork) for each request — isolated but heavy.
Each request is a thread — lighter than a process, shared memory.

os-boot-process.qsub: What is GRUB? What does the kernel do during initialization before launching the first process?
os-boot-process.what:
Power on → what happens?:

1. Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) — runs CPU boot code; performs hardware self-check; finds a bootable device.

2. Bootloader (GRUB) — loads the kernel image into RAM and hands over control (like giving control to main()).

3. Kernel init — sets up memory and paging, loads drivers, mounts the root file system.

4. init/systemd (PID 1) — first user-space process; starts the remaining services. Now you have a shell or desktop.
os-boot-process.analogy:
Running a computer = project kickoff:
1. Reception (firmware) — checks everything is OK, determines which team (device) is ready — selects the boot device.
2. Manager entrance (bootloader) — brings the manager (kernel) onto the stage, "take over now."
3. Manager (kernel) — sets up departments (memory, drivers), opens the office (rootfs).
4. Team lead (init/systemd) — all employees (services) start. Now work (shell) runs — "boot completed!"
os-boot-process.why: Understanding the boot chain = the OS’s “hello world” flow. In an interview, “what happens when you turn on a computer” shows the layered architecture: firmware → bootloader → kernel → user space. This clarifies concepts such as GRUB, BIOS, PID 1, and init.

Bootloader flexible (multi-OS/GRUB).
systemd starts services in parallel (fast).
cons: Any layer can fail (hard to debug).
Firmware/bootloader are vendor-specific.
systemd is controversial (complex).

Select "boot from USB" — chooses the boot chain.

os-program-execution.q: Explain what happens at the OS level when you run ./myprogram.
os-program-execution.what:
./myprogram running at OS level does what:

1. fork() — creates a new process (a copy of the parent). 2. exec() — replaces that process's image with myprogram. The loader reads the ELF file and maps code/data into memory, sets up stack+heap, and resolves dynamic libs (.so).

3. Control goes to the entry point — _start/main(). Now the program runs.

fork + exec: fork creates a new process, exec changes its image — a two-step Unix design.

Loader = HR that reads the CV (ELF) and sets up the desk (memory), paperwork (stack/heap), and the team (libraries), then calls the boss (main). Dynamic linking = “these managers share the library” — no repeated copies (saves RAM).
os-program-execution.why: In binary execution, three major OS fundamentals appear: fork vs exec (process creation), virtual memory mapping (loader), static vs dynamic linking. In an interview, the question "what happens when you run a program" tests these deep answers. This is how you understand the behavior of the shell, ./a.out, and libraries.

os-thrashing.q: What is thrashing? How does the OS detect and prevent it?
os-thrashing.qsub: What is the working set model? How does swappiness tuning affect server performance?
os-thrashing.what:
Thrashing — when the combined working sets of all processes exceed RAM. Each process’s page fault rate rises, the OS pulls a page from disk, but the page is needed again right away → constant paging, no computation.

Detect — page fault rate is very high, CPU utilization drops. Prevent — working set model: track each process’s active pages; if the sum > RAM then suspend some processes (or add memory). In Linux, swappiness controls the tendency to swap anonymous memory versus file cache.
os-thrashing.analogy: Overbooked gym: all members arrive at once (too many processes), each needs a machine (working set). If there’s no machine, everyone is waiting and waiting — no one is actually exercising (CPU idle), everyone is just looking for the “next machine” (faults/swap). Remedy: suspend some members (or expand the gym) — then the remaining can exercise (compute).
os-thrashing.why: High load or low RAM makes thrashing a real problem — the system feels like a "brick" (utilization drops, response stalls). Therefore understanding detection/prevention is essential: check the working set sum, monitor the fault rate, tune swappiness. This is a common "OS-level performance" interview question.
pros: Working set provides a clear model — easy to detect.
Suspend restores compute.
Swappiness knobs — tune manually.
gotchas: Just remember: thrashing = working sets sum > RAM → paging only, CPU idle. Detect via fault rate.
High si/so (swap in/out) in vmstat = red flag.
Interview: "How does the OS prevent thrashing?" — working set model, suspend, more RAM.

os-linux-internals.desc: /proc filesystem, cgroups, namespaces, copy-on-write — the building blocks of containers.
os-linux-internals.qsub: What is the /proc filesystem? What useful information can you extract from /proc/[pid]?
os-linux-internals.what:
Containers (Docker) are built on Linux kernels:

Namespaces — give processes separate views (PID, network, mount, user...). In one container PID 1, in another also PID 1 — each has its own "isolated system".

cgroups — resource limits (CPU %, memory max). A container does not take excessive RAM.

Copy-on-write — pages are shared (fast); they are copied only when written. Fork does not need to copy the binary.

/proc — kernel's virtual info: /proc/<pid>/ contains filenames, fd, memory, cmdline. OverlayFS — merges image layers, container-specific rootfs.

• Namespace = each flat gets its own "own flat" feel — everyone’s kitchen is 101 (PID 1), but they are separate (isolation). Network is also separate per flat.

• CoW = when moving in (fork), the furniture (pages) is not copied — only when it is modified.
• /proc = building’s info panel — who is where. Image = delivery blueprint.

In an interview, the answer to "how does Docker isolate?" is namespaces + cgroups; "what is /proc?" demonstrates practical Linux knowledge. CoW enables a performant fork. They connect modern infrastructure (containers) to the OS — high-signal interview material.

raid-levels.q: What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6? When would you choose each?
raid-levels.qsub: What is the rebuild time problem with large RAID 5 arrays? How does RAID 10 compare to RAID 5 for write-heavy workloads?
raid-levels.what:
RAID combines multiple disks to provide either speed, safety (or both). Levels differ in trade-offs:

RAID 0 — distributes data in stripes (blocks) across all disks. I/O runs in parallel → fast. But no redundancy — if one disk fails, all data is lost.

RAID 1 — stores a copy of each block on two disks. Fail-safe, but capacity is halved.

RAID 5 — stripe plus parity (recovery info). Can rebuild after one disk fails. RAID 6 — two parity blocks, tolerates two failures. RAID 10 — stripe of mirrored pairs = speed + safety (but requires twice as many disks).
raid-levels.analogy:
How to handle your important notes:
• RAID 0 = split the notes across two tables — both read fast, but if any table page is lost the note is half.
• RAID 1 = full copy on both tables — even if one table burns, you still have the note.
• RAID 5 = notes plus a "check-sum" note — if one table fails, the check-sum lets you reconstruct the rest.
• RAID 10 = two copies of each note in pairs, arranged for speed — best performance but expensive.
raid-levels.why: Storage decisions depend on requirements: speed (RAID 0), safety (RAID 1), balance (RAID 5/6), best-of-both (RAID 10). Rebuild time for large arrays and the write cost of parity are key considerations when choosing production storage. This is the answer for HA design.

mmap.qsub: What are the disadvantages of mmap? How does it interact with the page cache?
mmap.what:
mmap — map a file as if it were part of virtual memory. File read/write behaves like memory array read/write (pointer).

OS page cache manages — file pages reside in memory, access is immediate. Write-back: changes are written lazily to disk (msync forces). On a page fault demand load — not the whole file, only the needed part.

vs read/write: there a user-space buffer copy occurs + a syscall each time. mmap reduces copies (memory-mapped access), large files become efficient.
mmap.analogy: Reading a large book (file): read/write = request each page from the librarian, who provides a copy (syscall + copy). mmap = keep the book open on your desk (map) — read/write directly, no copy. When a page is needed (demand) — open it. Write your edits (write-back) on the book, and when you wish, use msync to "shelve" it (force to disk).
mmap.why: For large files / random access / shared pages mmap is efficient — no per-read syscall copy. Page cache is reused. Hence databases (page cache), loaders (map binary), memory-mapped I/O are common. But predictability is lower — page faults and memory pressure (OOM) are problematic. storage-devices.q: What is the difference between HDD, SSD, and NVMe at the hardware level?
storage-devices.what:
HDD — actual spinning disk + magnetic head. The head must move to the data track (seek) = slow ~5-10ms. Sequential is fast (one wave), random is slow (head moves each time).

SSD — NAND flash, no moving parts, no seek — random also fast. But write amplification: flash erases at page-block level, so even a small write erases a large area, adding wear.

NVMe — SSD over PCIe — 4–10× faster than SATA, multiple queues, deep queue depth.

TRIM — marks a deleted block as free (extends SSD lifespan). I/O scheduler: HDD needs a scheduler (SCAN), NVMe does not — none/deadline.
storage-devices.analogy: Library: HDD = a librarian who walks to the shelf for a book (seek). Nearby books (sequential) are fast; far books (random) are slow. SSD = books on chips where no walking is needed — any book is immediate (random fast), but writing a chapter requires erasing the whole page-block (write amplification). NVMe = think of a super-fast conveyor. TRIM = "this page is free" sign — makes writing easier.
storage-devices.why: Understanding modern storage choices: latency (NVMe <<< SSD < HDD), cost/GB, write pattern, wear. These drive system design, database, and caching decisions. Knowing SSD wear/write amplification is essential for selecting the right solution for write-heavy workloads (optane / log).
gotchas: Just remember: HDD seek = slow random; SSD no seek but write amp; NVMe fastest (PCIe); TRIM extends lifespan.
Write amplification = even a small write triggers a block erase — memory wear.
Interview: "why is NVMe hot?" — PCIe, more queues/parallelism, low latency.

NAND flash, no seek — random fast, write amplification.

demand-paging.qsub: What is thrashing and how do you detect it? How does the working set model prevent thrashing?
demand-paging.what:
Demand paging — when a program starts, it does not load the entire memory; whenever a page is accessed and it is not in RAM, it is fetched from disk via a page fault. This saves memory and makes startup fast (only necessary pages).

Each process’s working set = pages that are actively used. If the sum of all working sets exceeds RAM → thrashing (a fault on every access, CPU idle). The remedy is working-set control plus page replacement (LRU/Clock). Colocation/over-subscription revolve around this.
demand-paging.analogy: Imagine a large library (program) you want to read: the whole library is not brought in at once (demand paging). You look (access) at tables 3, 7, 12 — only those are fetched (page fault). The books you are currently using = working set. If all readers (processes) together request 100 books but the library has only 50 tables (RAM) — you have to switch tables each time (thrashing) and no one can actually read.
demand-paging.why: Memory is limited and programs are large — demand paging enables large programs on small RAM with fast startup. But over-subscription leads to thrashing — a severe performance hit. Working set + LRU/Clock + over-subscribe knobs form the core of production memory management. This answers interview questions like "why is startup fast" and "what is thrashing".

Startup fast — without reading everything.
Large programs on small RAM.
gotchas: Just remember: demand paging = load on access (page fault). working set = active pages. sum > RAM = thrashing.
vmstat si/so high → thrashing signal.
Interview: "startup fast?" — lazy page load, only necessary.

The accessed page is not in RAM → the system fetches it from disk.

posix-threads.desc: pthreads is the C/POSIX thread API. pthread_create, pthread_join, pthread_mutex_lock, pthread_cond_wait. Portable across Unix/Linux/macOS. Foundation for understanding OS-level threading. Java threads and Go goroutines build on OS threads which use pthreads on Unix.
posix-threads.q: How do you create and join a thread using pthreads? What are the key differences from Java threads?
posix-threads.what:
pthreads = C's POSIX thread API — the standard for creating OS threads on Unix/Linux/macOS.

pthread_create — creates a thread; pthread_join — waits for it to finish. Sharing: threads share the same heap/code (unlike processes). Therefore a mutex is necessary — to prevent races on shared data.

Condition variables — a thread waits until another thread gives a "ready" signal (pthread_cond_wait/signal). Spurious wakeup: the wait can wake up without a signal — so always wait inside a while loop, not in an if.

Java threads / Go goroutines run on internal OS threads (pthreads on Unix) — this is the foundation.
posix-threads.analogy:
Imagine a kitchen team:
• pthread_create = hire a new cook.
• pthread_join = the head chef waits until the cook finishes the task.
• Mutex = a single stove (shared); only one cook can use it at a time — lock it so two cooks don’t burn the food (race).
• Cond var = the cook signals "food ready"; another waits — but a "false alarm" (spurious) can occur, so check again with a while loop to confirm the food is truly ready.
posix-threads.why: pthreads = fundamentals of OS-thread programming. Concurrency, race conditions, synchronization (mutex/condvar) all happen here. Java/Go “virtual” threads also run on OS threads — so understanding the OS thread model is essential. Interview questions often include "what is a thread? mutex? deadlock? condvar? spurious?" — all stem from this.

Locks a critical section — prevents races.
